## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

In the morning, choose one small intention: "Today I will notice one hook before I act from it." You might already have a guess about which one it'll be. Any hook will do, though, whichever one shows up. At night, look back over the day without putting yourself on trial. Where did you notice the hook, and where did it run its whole sequence anyway?

Noticing counts as progress, even if it's only now, looking back, that you think "oh, that was a hook." If you interrupted the pattern somewhere, notice that too. What's the next small repair, or something protective you can do? And what moment of warmth or pleasure did you actually get? Or it might have been a moment of courage, or of connection. Repair what can be repaired and renew the intention, and then go to sleep.

## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.

But a big spiritual experience can show you a kind of peace, or a love, you didn't know existed, and then "I want you to be happy" suddenly means something much bigger. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost comically simple to someone who's never been near what it's pointing at, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying "may you be happy" over and over isn't automatically some profound love. It's one way of finding that deeper love and growing it.

If you're curious about that bigger happiness, follow the curiosity instead of pretending to believe something. Read people from different traditions, and meet people whose lives make you wonder. You might already know someone like that, who's happy in a way you can't quite figure out. And judge a path by its fruits: what are the people who follow it like?

Sometimes care isn't what's missing. The whole horizon of life feels too small, and the question underneath is "Why should I want this life at all?" (or however it sounds in your head). A meal or a boundary can help without touching the question. So can a kind sentence. Take that question seriously. Maybe right now life is just something you get through. What would have to be possible for being alive to feel worth discovering?

Curiosity can be enough here, something like "Other people say they've felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don't know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?" Don't assume the limits of what you've felt so far are the limits of what's possible.
t65z3_secsp8m8:
## Use Childhood Photographs Without Interrogating Them

Some people can't picture their little one without feeling like they're making the whole thing up. If that's you, find an actual photo from back then. The face is already there, and so is however you were standing, so there's nothing to invent. You may not have looked at it in years. Look at it gently, notice what comes up, and try not to decide ahead of time what the picture is supposed to prove.

While you look, notice what your body does and what feelings or urges show up, and what that younger you seems to want you to get. Then sort it. Some of it you'll remember yourself, and some of it someone told you later ("You hated that coat"). Some you're guessing from the picture, and some might be an image or a dream, or you honestly don't know. Then ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

And try not to ask it leading questions, like "What abuse must have happened?", "Who did this to me?" or "What memory is my body hiding?" Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but not necessarily a true one. Guided imagery and suggestive questions can create false memories. [In one study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03196318), people shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took started remembering it, about half of them, at least partly.

A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed. It doesn't show what was happening outside the frame, or why you looked the way you did that day. So it can tell you something real about how you feel now, the way a dream can, and still prove nothing about the story it seems to tell. Same goes for a jolt in your body when you look at it.

If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don't confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here. You might be looking at the photo thinking, "That would explain so much." Write down exactly what came up and how it came up, and get some support from someone level-headed who won't lead you toward an answer.

Put the photo back in its drawer when you're finished, good day or not. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you're getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present first, the way you usually would.

# When Love Still Feels Missing

If you weren't loved well as a child, "love your inner child" can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn't close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.

Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It's scaffolding, and it isn't a test of whether you were loved enough.

Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you've never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won't let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it's been heard (see the section Hear the Protective Part First).

# If You Want to Kill Yourself

Maybe you're reading this with a plan, or the means, close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line or an emergency number counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger. Do the same if you can't stop yourself, or you're badly disoriented or intoxicated. Can't tell if that's you? Treat it like it is. This isn't me answering whether life is worth living. It just keeps the question open long enough to look at.

Then ask: what is the self you want to kill? Is that self the same thing as your body? Why? Do you have the same body in dreams? What exactly do you expect your body's death to accomplish? If the problem is a state of mind, like self-hatred or despair, shame or loneliness, what makes you so sure that destroying the body ends it?

Buddhism, for what it's worth, doesn't treat death as an off switch, or as a free get-out-of-jail card back to the source. It says repeated thought and intention shape the mind, that this keeps going through death and rebirth, that hell realms are possible, and that a human birth is a rare shot at understanding suffering and ending its causes. You don't have to believe any of that.

You can see that momentum within this life, too. Rumination feeds rumination, and isolation can deepen despair. The more you hate yourself, the better your mind gets at it. Physical life keeps handing you redirections, though, like other people and things you have to do, and help when you reach for it. If the many traditions and the accumulating scientific evidence are right that the mind's causal process goes on after the body dies, killing the body may take away some of those redirections without taking away the suffering.

So, if everything's already on the table, what's the change you still can't bring yourself to make? Leaving? Quitting? Moving? Telling your family who you really are? Those aren't free, and you can't always take them back, but they're smaller than dying, and they can wait until you're calmer and have some help. Look at that life you've been afraid to change while you still have a human body, and people around to help redirect the path.
